blocks.x: Just tell your name and where you were born and when.

My name is John Handy. I was born in Paschke, San, Mississippi in 1900. The exact day? The 24th day of June. I made the 25th day of June of 58. I've been fooling around with music since I was 10 years old.
Were your family musical? Everybody. What about your father, mother and your grandfather now?

Well, I don't know my grandfather. He died before I was big enough to know him. But my daddy played violin. My mother was a pianist. My sister's a pianist. My brother's a guitarist. And I got one player's bass. The one player's guitarist named Julius Handy. My sister's named Mary Louise Handy. My mother's name is Elizabeth Handy. My daddy's name is John Handy Sr.
What did you say your daddy played? Violin.

Violin? Violin stuff You take a round out of one of those chairs and you put your finger down like this. And you saw it with the round and it sounded just like a bass violin. Your finger rubs across the round? No, you take the stick and rub across right here.
Oh, a stick. And it goes... And it goes like a bass.

Just like a bass violin. And when my dad used to be rehearsing like that, I'd get my stick and get on the porch. Played bass with her. Then I started playing guitar. From there I played mandolin. From there I played a little bass. Then I become a drummer. Played drums about... We were, I see, for about six years.
What about guitar? How did you play with pigs? Yeah, yeah, pigs. What kind of pigs? Oh, cellar pigs. Would it be a flat pick or a plum pick? Yeah, flat. Flat pick.
Flat pick. Oh, there was a picker. I never had a pick. I had this chord.
You played chords in mandolin. How did you play that? With a flat pick? Yeah.

Played lead on that. I played in mandolin. My brother, Jujus, was playing guitar. And my brother was playing bass, Sylvester. And we had a nice trio. We used to make a lot of money. We used to go around serenading people at the different hotels in Paris Christiane, Luxie, Gulfport. We used to go all around, I think. And, uh, serenading. Go from house to house. We made nice money. Sometimes we used to come back seven, five, eighty dollars. A night. We used to make nice money, I think. Oh, from drums, I wanted to play clarinet. And I had a fellow over there. There was a white fellow. He was a barber. His name is Piku Luzander. He was a clarinet player, and I just liked the way he played it. And I never fooled with clarinet. But, uh, I heard him playing. And I got interested in playing the clarinet. So I kept after my dad at a bar when he kept telling me he wasn't able. Well, I was working. I'd take my own money and buy it, but he wouldn't let me. So, uh, he went up and talked to Piku. And, uh, Piku got him one. And he gave it to me. Well, that one was brand new when he gave me.
Remember what kind?

It was an apple. And, uh, so he told my daddy to give him the brand new one. Because it was hard to work. He was telling me. It was brand new. And he know more about it than I did. And he swapped it for his own. Well, this one was in perfect condition. I was willing because, uh, that one was hard to blow with the brand new ones. So he swapped me. And I never taken a lesson in my life. I just taken the clarinet and sit on the porch in the evening when I come from work or get in the room. And figure out note for note. If I could get make, I could make three notes. Then I'd go look for another note until I learned the whole horn like that. Just note for note, feeling for him until I found him. So I commenced to playing a tune. Anything I could whistle, then I could play it on the clarinet. Well, I played around there for, I'd say about a year and a half.
What age were you then when you started clarinet?

I was around, I was around 17 years old. 16 or 17 years old when I started playing clarinet. And then various bands used to come from here over there. And when they'd come, I'd bring my clarinet. You'd swear I was going to work out. Bring my clarinet. Peter go in. This is big. They have my clarinet with me. I'd get in there and I'd beg them to let me play with them. Sometime they'd turn me down and sometime they'd let me play. But after you let me play once, then they wouldn't have no trouble. I wouldn't have no trouble asking them no more. They'd be begging me to come play then. Well, that's why I used to start playing then.
Who were some of those guys?
Well, I used to play with Punch Miller. He'd come over there. I used to play with Dude Foster. He'd come over there. Rene.
Now who is Dude Foster? Is that the trumpet player? Yeah. What, did he have a brother?
Yeah, he played trombone.
Oh, wow. I just wanted to get him straight. Yeah. So I'd know who he was.

Uh-huh. Then I played with Rene and he'd come over there. As a matter of fact, I played with Rene here. But he first known me from over there. Uh, when Jim Robson used to come over there with Sam Morgan, I was a little boy then. And he used to come over there with Sam Morgan when I used to play with him. And then Isaiah Morgan made up him a band. He used to come over there. He used to play with him. I played with Isaiah a long time. And then Tom Albert come to play with my daddy. Well, he told me I was a heard me playing. As a matter of fact, I played with him. Several times he'd come over there to play with my daddy. And, uh, he thought I was a sensation. So he asked my daddy to let me come over here with him and play with him. So he agreed. And I come here around 1928. Around 1918, rather. And I started playing with Tom Albert. And I had a lot of opportunities to go with different bands, but... I don't know. I always thought of Tom as my daddy. He's a fine old man. I just stuck with him. I had plenty of opportunities to leave him, but... He couldn't play much, but he was a nice fellow.
What kind of cornet did he play? Did he play straight or hard?
No, he was a more musical type. He was a straight trumpet player.
Did he get off at all? Uh-uh. Had to have the music in front of him.
Unless it's something he'd been playing about three or four years.
And then could he marry it? Did he play it? No, no.
Just like it was written. Just like it was written. Note for note. He couldn't play nothing else but note for note. He was a great brass band man, too. Yeah, he's a great writer.
Who did he play with?

Oh, him and Peter Bocard then used to play together on those parades. I think it was the... I think Solastain had a brass band at that time, and they were playing together, and he was a member of the band. But I didn't like that. You didn't like that? No, I didn't like that. Couldn't get me out there. I didn't want to play. Now, sometime when a musician would die like that, or René and them would get together and just build up a band. No pay, just play behind him, you know what I mean? I'd go out there, something like that. But Peter Bocard then was playing, that was too much for me. I was playing strictly about music, and I wasn't...I didn't know nothing about notes or nothing like that at that time. So I stayed out of that.
How long were you with Tom Alvin? How many years?

I was with Tom for about, let's say five, six years. Matter of fact, I was with him from 1918 up to 1924. 1924. 1924, I got married in 1923. 1924, I left here and went to Baton Rouge with Titt Johnson's off string. He had one of the leading bands outside of New Orleans. It was Bud Scott out of Natchez, and Williams out of Napoleonville, Donisonville.
What was Bud Scott playing at the time? Which instruments?
He wasn't playing no instruments at that time. He wasn't? Mm-mm. What did he do?
Sing.
Oh.
Bud never did play no instruments. Oh.
You might be talking, you might think I'm talking about Bud Scott the guitar player, but I'm just talking... Yeah.
Oh, well there's two different guys.
Yeah, I'm talking about Bud Scott out of Natchez, Mississippi. He had a band, but he didn't do nothing but sing.
And, uh, to Bud Scott the guitar player, where was he from?
I don't know Bud Scott the guitar player. I'm up hood of him, but I don't know him.
That's always been confusing. I mean, that's news.

Yeah, Bud Scott here, uh, a year of taking care of part of Mississippi out to Northern Port, all of Louisiana, practically. Well, he was big as that sign then. Uh-huh. He was way around 207. He was a great big man, and he would sing without a microphone. You know, at them times they didn't have these. And one of them things used to sing through like... A megaphone? Yeah. He didn't sing through that.
He'd just stand up and shout. Just stand up and sing.
Uh-huh. And he had bosses over someplace he'd go enjoy the building. He was a big powerful guy. What would he sing?
What kind of numbers? Anything they'd play.
He'd sing. It was his bands, you know. They'd rehearsal together. But he would sing popular songs? Yeah. He'd sing a lot of popular songs. Some jump numbers.
He'd sing a lot of waltzes. And then there was time waltzes was awful popular.

And he'd sing a lot of them. Did a lot of singing. But he didn't play anything. Oh, he had a playhouse in his yard, though. That thing was around 12 by 12 was a little girl. He had a real funny to play. He was a great guy. He was a great guy. for his little girl. They had real furniture in there too, but that was just the playhouse there. He had a wonderful home over there. Well, there was the three leading orchestras outside of New Orleans. It was Bud Scott, Claiborne William, and Tut Johnson. Claiborne William out of Donaldsonville, Tut Johnson out of Baton Rouge, and Bud Scott out of Natchez. Well, they was doing all the business out there, and I was with Tut. And I stayed with Tut from 24 until 26. Then I left Tut and went with the Tony Harris. Who was with Tut at that time? Tut Johnson had at that time Clarence Thompson on drum, Euless Jarrou on trumpet, Dimes on
trumpet. Which Dimes was this?

A little Wesley Dimes. He's dead now. He got killed. And he had Robert. They called him Bob. He plays around here. He plays on the, he's kind of sick now. He waits down here at the first precinct. You know Bob. He played trombone. So he recorded with, uh... Bob Thomas? Yeah. He recorded with Bob Ryan. He recorded with several orchestra friends. Yeah. But he was playing trombone at the time.
And is he from Baton Rouge or something? I think Bob is from Baton Rouge. He's out in California now, you know. Is he? Yeah.
Yeah. I thought he was still working downtown.
No, I want to see him if I get out there. Oh yeah. Well, Tut was a guitar player. Tut Johnson,

he was a guitar player. He was playing guitar. He had a fella by the name of Mal playing bass. Now I got killed. One night, we was coming from White Castle. A fella dropped and ran into our car and hit the back wheel and turned us over. And, uh, turned us over three times in the middle of the street. And I was sitting right side of Mal. We was sitting on that side and I was sitting in the middle. And along the build tunnel and busted his bass all up. Killed him. Didn't kill him right. Then we take him to a black man to a hospital. And when he got there, he was dead.
Then from Toody Johnson I went with Toody Harris. Now he was another singer. He didn't play nothing.
I don't know him.

No, I don't think you know him. Toody Harris, he was a big fella too. He was around 200 pounds. Well then Toody Harris' band they had Lyle Thompson on drums. Lurt Fritz on trombone. We had Ed Collins on trumpet. Guy Kelly on trumpet. Joe Robich on piano. Poise Sevilla on guitar. And I was playing clarinet. Clarence Hall was playing tenor saxophone. And a fella by the name of, what was his name? Oh I forget his name. But then he was on alto.
Where was that? No, it was in Baton Rouge. Oh. No, it was in Baton Rouge.

Then I stayed with Toody Harris about a year. Eight months a year. I got a telegram that my wife fixed to be operated on on a Saturday. And I got the telegram that Friday evening. And that's when I left that Friday evening. Come here. And uh... That Monday I went to work at the humming board. No, I played at the entertainers. I played at the entertainers for about six, eight months. And then we left there and... I went to the humming board. And that's where I sent for Guy Kelly, trumpet player. Sent for him. And he come down there. We stayed at the humming board until it closed. And that's when Stretchford used to come off the boot. Used to come up and hear me play clarinet. And he would never come inside. He'd sit outside all the time. In his car. I would never know he'd be out there. But somebody come in and tell me he's out there. Him and his wife and his brother. Used to come out there and sit down and just let him play. Fate Marble was playing with him at that time on the boot. And uh... He asked Fate to bring me out there. One night. I went out there. Stayed out there. I stayed out there. Played out there with him until he got ready to make the trip and leave. Well, I couldn't go on that trip. He didn't come back until twelve o'clock. I had to come back to work. I was just a boy. Well, I played that matinee with him. And uh... I had to leave him come back to work until six to pull out. But he wanted me to join the band. Go back up to St. Louis. But that boot job was a little bit too hard. You get up in the morning at 6.30. Eat breakfast in your oasis for two hours. Eat lunch. And you go back. Rehearsal about two more hours. And you rest and go back to work that night. Uh... Too much. I didn't like all that playing. Of course I liked to play, but I didn't like that much playing. Just to be playing to the empty walls like that. So I told him no.
I didn't think I wanted to go. I was doing alright there by the hummingbird. But anyway...
We stayed there for quite a number of years. And I left there and went to... Navita Dance Hall. On Aubrey Street. Between Rampart and Ugundy.
And I stayed there several years. Oh, who all was in the hummingbird? Guy Kelly?

You said? I had Guy Kelly on the trumpet. Song된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된 If you play with Sam Morgan you might see his pictures of his band. And George Gano on the banjo. That was all of us.
And you were playing clarinet at the time?
Yeah clarinet. I was playing clarinet at the time.
Where was the hummingbird?
The hummingbird was on Bienville and Marie.
What kind of place was going on in that neighborhood?
It was a little nightclub.
Was it district wide open then? Yeah. This was 20 o'clock, December 20th.
Yeah that was in the 20s. That was around 28.
Around 28. Yeah. Things would jump on there.
Oh yeah. Wide open then. Everything. Gathering, district, everything. It was right down there in the district.
Did they have any girls turning tricks in the place?
No not in the place.
Dancing?

There was a lot of dancing and drinking. The thing about it was when them girls come out of them cribs. They go home and take their bath and straighten their self up and put on them clothes. And come out there and just throw away some money.
Uh huh.

And all them pimps they just come right along there and just burn up money. And I enjoyed when they get off too. I liked it. I liked it. See they wanted nothing for them to come up there and give you four or five dollars a clear number. Yeah believe me you said such a thing. Thank you. What you drinking? So and so and so. Here. Send the weed up there. They have a lot of fun like that. I didn't like that.
What kind of numbers did the girls like?

Well they didn't have anything particular. I just liked a lot of ragtime stuff, jump stuff. I didn't like nothing too slow. Bless me was the blues. Now if you could play the blues for them all night they didn't like that. Just nothing but the blues but nothing slow like stardust or something like that. They didn't like nothing like that. That was too slow they didn't want that. But if you play the blues in that temple right down the alley they liked that. They used to uh get off from work around. And they did a lot of work around. One thirty two o'clock. Every time they got tired I mean. I mean. I just closed up that driven. I go in home and clean their self up. I put on their clothes. I get them a cab. I. I. I. I. I. I. I. I. I. I. I. I. I. I. dance hall we used to play over there. Go to work at 8 o'clock at night and work until 2 or 2.30 in the morning. But the dance hall music never stopped there. See one number right behind the other. We had music like that. We put it on a music stand and start from number one. I guess we played 300 and some numbers a night. Trump would take the first chorus and I take the second chorus. While I'm playing my chorus he turned over number one. He's ready to play number two. We need him to go out together and pick up number two. While he's picking up number two I turn over number one and put number two up. That goes on all night long. When he gets ready to go to lunch, he goes to lunch. I pick up the fourth chorus. Joe Robichaud would take the second. I take the third one out. Then I pick up the fourth. Then I pick up the next chorus. He take the second. Go on and out. For him, some numbers Jim could play. When I pick up Jim Robichaud would take the second chorus. I'd always have to pick up the first chord when the trumpet was gone. When he come back then either one wanted to go to the next. We'd ordinate like that until all of us went to lunch at night. Stayed for half an hour, an hour. Come back. Start back the week again. I stayed there for, oh lord I guess, six or seven years. In that place I had Lee Collins on trumpet. John Marrero on guitar. No, he was playing banjo. His brother on bass. Joe Robichaud on piano.
Is that Simon or Eddie Marrero on which one? Simon. Simon was on bass.

And drums? Drummer was Alfred William. And yourself, what were you playing then? I was playing clarinet. Still? No, I was playing saxophone then. Yeah, because I started fooling with saxophone when I was at the hummingbird.
What year did you start fooling with saxophone? Oh, around 29. 28, 29, somewhere. And how come you took up saxophone?

Well that was all that was playing around here at that time. I didn't give up clarinet. When I wanted to, one man I wanted to meet with clarinet was Sidney Bessier. Uh huh. But I never got a chance to play against Sidney because he was in New York. He left a week before I come here. I never got a chance to even hear him play, but on records that's all. But I sure wanted to play against Sidney. He said, when I went to Baton Rouge, I met a fella up there called Green. He had Baton Rouge sewed up in clarinet. Man, that cat would play some clarinet. But after I was up there about six months, he was just another clarinet man.

Who was that guy in Baton Rouge that didn't have any keys on his clarinet? Did you know him? No. That was strange. That's how he could play. Any number you wanted, but he just fingered the holes was all. Stopped everything else up, just used those three fingers on each hand.

I don't know who that was. It beats me. I don't know how he did it. Unless it was Green. They had some nice clarinet players up there now. They were strictly musicians. They couldn't get off at all. Just played strictly music. I had a fella up there by the name of Titten Knox had a band up there. They were fine musicians as well. They were arranging and played that stuff. They sounded good. They really sounded good. But they played strictly about their music. They kept pretty busy too.
What about Victor? Did you know him up there?

Yeah, Victor. He was a trumpet player. He was stout. He had a brother who played violin. He was a great man with one of those little tomato cans. He was trumpet. He was great with that. Fine, trying guy. Was he a, what you'd call a ratty musician?
Huh? Was he ratty in his style?
Yeah, yeah. He could get off. That bucket, huh? Yeah, he could get off pretty good. Yeah, a lot of stuff.
Was Tith Johnson's band, would you call that a pretty ratty band too, or was it mostly?

No, at times it was pretty jumpy. And this boy, Wesley Dimes, and the drummer, and myself, we'd make it pretty jumpy at times. That fellow leading Tith Johnson's band, his name was Oil. I know Lawrence. He was a crippled guy. One leg short another. He was a violin player. Or he could write to. He had Tith Johnson a good band though. Very good band, cause he could write a lot of stuff. He was a fine musician. And he was a violin player. When he could stand up, he'd be drunk all the time. He could, he'd sit in. He'd sit down and go to sleep. He'd sit down and go to sleep. Then. He he he he. But he'd make you play that music right then. And keep that in your mind. Until he'd go to sleep. Then after he'd go to sleep. Then we'd play like we want. Then break up the house. He he he he.
Didn't any of the musicians around here have a drink?

Around here? Uh huh. Oh. Man. Drink. Used to drink myself. That's the only way I could play. Drink. Yeah. That's the only way I could play. To drink. If I didn't have nothing to drink. That was it. I remember when I was playing to the Lovito. I used to go to work every night with a quarter whiskey. Every night. To have a quarter whiskey. I bought so much whiskey at the Waldorf drugstore. Until I wouldn't have to tell the man what I want. When they see me come to sleep.
come in to do it, grab the bottle and wrap it up. Give it to me. Get it all credit, I didn't have no money all the time. Get it all credit. Pee him when I get off.
When you moved to the city, where did you live? What neighborhood?

I lived on Dauphin and St. Louis. Right with Tom Albert, right in his house with his wife. His little girl. They were same as my people. I lived right there with them. Go out and then we moved from there to Rightways Living. How about that? 635 Bagan Street. Right around the corner. We moved from there and we didn't have no truck either. Got everything around there by hand. He had a gallon of whiskey. And a clothes basket of sandwiches. And everybody we seen on the street. You want a drink? Yeah. Come on. Go get a piece of furniture and bring it around. We give you a drink. That's the way we moved. Everybody seen on the street thought they'd drink. They'd offer them a drink but they had to bring a piece of furniture for us before they get a drink. They had to give him a drink. They had a fine wife. They had a fine wife. Miss Louise was a very fine woman. Miss Louise was a very fine woman.
She's dead now? She's dead now?

Yeah, she's dead poor soul. She made Tom what he used to do. Because Tom used to work out there on the riverfront. Then he used to be a trapper. In the wintertime he'd do a lot of trapping and he made a lot of money. But if he'd leave him keeping, he'd throw it away.
See?

And she'd taken that money and bought that house. She got it right there down. And uh, furnished it off. And when she died, she left him, she left him a lot of money. I don't know if he still got it, but she, I'd say a lot, she left him about twelve, fourteen thousand dollars. And she died. And he don't have to spend that money because he got everything in that house.
Now you were saying who you had in the band and the La Vida, too. We were just talking about it.
No, I said Alcon played with me at La Vida after Lee Connors left my Chicago. Him and John Marrero went to Chicago. And then Alcon and George Gano coming.
Now was that after, was that after Collins worked at the Astoria with Davy Jones? Or do you know?
And that was, um, oh, matter of fact, David Jones played at the La Vida with me, too.
Well, they were together at the, at the Astoria. Yeah.
And I wondered if that was before.
And I wondered if that was before. No, I think that was after they left the Astoria. Mm-hmm.

They would often come down there with me, out to La Vida. Well, I think John, uh, Lee Collins and John Marrero left for, uh, left, uh, a tenor player there. Yeah, they went to Chicago and left him there. And they went to Chicago and left him there. And David Jones stayed there with me a long time. As a matter of fact, he opened up, uh, a teacher school uptown here somewhere. here some way. Alfred Williams stayed there a long time. Jim Robinson stayed there a long time. But uh, Alfred left and went to Texas. And Robinson and I stayed there until the police closed down. Who took Alfred's class? Who was playing drums there? I can't remember who played drums there after I left now. Oh yeah, Papa. Little fella called Papa. I don't know his other name. He died here about three years ago. He was playing with Paju and them at the next door to La Vida.
Is that the sort of Mexican looking fella? Yeah, yeah, that's him. I think Andy Anderson was talking about that.
Yeah, that's him.
Oh yeah.

Yeah, he died here about three years ago. I think he taking Alfred's place with me at the La Vida. But after I left the La Vida, then I organized me a large band. I had the person named Hannes Louisiana Shakers. Well, I had Willie Pacho on the first trumpet. I had Rick R. Alexis on the second trumpet. I had Robert on the trombone. I had George Clark on the tenor. My cell phone alto. I had a little fella playing alto. He dropped the date up at Jackson and Germany. What was his name? I think it's his name in a minute. I had H.A. Minor on the guitar. I had Old Man Kimball on the bass. Raymond Doyce on the piano. Roy Evans on drums. No vocalists. Didn't have nobody singing. At that time, singers wasn't doing so well. Just instrument, you know. Instrument band. Singers wasn't doing so much. We did a lot of work. We worked out at Fourth Way, Texas. Beaumont. Ascended Torn. Houston. Galveston. Florida. Pensacola. Alabama. Alabama. We played a place I did called Chickasaw, Alabama. Played Mobile a lot of times. I'm Biloxi. Guffbo. Pash Christian. Place is called Franklinton out here on the other side of Bugaloosa. We played Bugaloosa over three or four times a month. We played against Celestan at the Roosevelt Hotel. After that, I lost all my music.
What happened?

Oh, we was coming from Bugaloosa. And we played a dance up there that Saturday night. We had this contest with Celestan on Sunday night at the Roosevelt. And we put the music on the running boat or somewhere. The piano player was in charge of it. And he forgot to tie it or something like that. We got into the slide there. I missed the music. And they asked him, I put it on the hood. On the hood. No music. Eleven of us. I let them out at the white kitchen and I went back. All the way back to Bugaloosa looking for my music. Never did find it. I put a hand in the paper for it. Never did find my music. I did. And a lot of that music, practically all of it, Louis Armstrong had sent it to me. Out of Chicago. He had sent me that music. Matter of fact, he sent me a little trunk of music. And I lost it all.
Who had the arrangement? Was it stock?

He had some arrangement and a lot of stock, but he had a lot of arrangements in there. I don't know who did the arrangement, but he had a lot of arrangements. He had a number like, they arranged called Boku Jack, McCarty Chop Suey, Nine In The Shed, all them kind of numbers. It was hard, hard stuff to play. Yeah, I had several more up in there. Sally Trombone had an arrangement on that. That was one of them old Scott Joblin numbers though. You know, but Louis had an arrangement, or somebody arranged it for him. And he sent me that. And I lost all that music. And I was like, I'm sorry. But we went up there, went on up there. Blindfolded, we did all right too. I wasn't calling nothing, but numbers I knew there was no customer playing. They could memorize it. And I wasn't trying to play nothing. Out of ordinary, just straight stuff. Because I knew if we tried to, you know, play something about music, it would make a humbug. Everybody would get confused. Just something we all was familiar with, straight. And played that.
And did nice up there.

And then I went by World Iron. I got about $75 of all of us music. Rehearsing that, we got it down. And we had a contest with, what's his name, William there, or Donaldsonville, Claiborne Weave. And we had a contest with, up at Pelican. We had so many people in there, you couldn't get nobody else in the place. They would line it out all on the side, all around the building they would line it, but you couldn't get nobody else in there. Then the next contest we had was the-
Well, who won these contests? Let me tell you, what about Claiborne Williams and all that? How'd you come out?

He had a, Claiborne Williams had a fine band, really a fine band. But I was blowing so much horn in them times that his band didn't count too much. I was breaking up the house, and where I went, I was tearing up out there. I was young, and I liked it to play, and could play, and I just went on to up everything. All I wanted was a piano and a drum behind me. I didn't need nothing else. I was playing. I was playing. And, uh...
People liked what? What did they want you to play? What would you win the contest with? Anything.

I didn't have anything. Did you hit the waltz? Oh yeah, I had that waltz sometime. I made a big hit with that. I used to play that all the time, a lot of times. They would request that waltz four and five times a night, sometime. There was a waltz where we used to, uh... The reeds would get off the stand and walk around the hall, one behind the other. I played that in three-part harmony. I would come back and walk back on the stand, and then the brass would get on, and go around and do the same thing. We'd come back and we'd all go out together. That was a beautiful waltz. I used to break up the house with it. They would play that thing three or four times before they'd let us stop playing it. It was a pretty waltz. And then it had a nice range on it.
Well, when you had a contest, would the other band play the same tune or what? How would that work?

No, no. They'd play what they want. They'd play what they wanted. They'd play the best they got. They'd play what they wanted to. You don't have to play just what they play. Sometimes accidentally you play a number they played already, or they're going to play, something like that. But you don't have to play. You just play what you think you can play best. Best super for your band, that's what you play. Because tonight I played against Earl Hines down there. And Earl Hines had a good band in them days. He was a wonderful piano player, then he had a good band. He won that contest too. Now Earl Hines here broke out there. Matter of fact, he had everybody out to dance all over there on his stand. He was a good band. But I didn't do that. I don't break out and start the playing right off the reel. I didn't let the other fella have a little fun for a while. Then I'm... ...

take me a couple of shots and I begin to call some numbers. I'll begin to blow a little bit. Take me a couple of more shots. And just give me that drum, that piano, and bass. Then I'll get the people over here. Just clap your hand, I'll bring the people here. Well around 1.30 I had Earl Hines over there, let alone all the people. Had him over there. Him and his whole band, because I know that boy was playing first alto with him, I knew him better. He's a fine guy, he played violin too.
Who was that?
I forget his name now, but he's a fine violin player.
Was that Donnell Howard? Would that be the point?
No, it wasn't Howard. Not in them times. Oh, I see.
Mundy, Jerry? Not Jerry Mundy.
No, it wasn't Mundy. I know Mundy. He was a kind of heavyset brown skinned fellow. Kind of Indian looking for him.
By the way, when did you first meet Louis Armstrong?
I met Louis around 19, 19, 19, 20. He was waiting right around the corner from me.
Oh yeah?
Yeah, he was waiting on Ramport between Canal and Iberville, and I was waiting on Iberville between Ramport and Burgundy.
What places were these?
At that time that was the E-Light, E-Light Nightclub.
And who was there, which one? He was in the E-Light or he was there?
No, he was at Tom Anderson around the nightclub, and I was at the E-Lights. I was waiting for Beansy for a day then.
Beansy on the E-Light?
Yeah.
I didn't know that.
Yeah, that was his place. I was waiting for Beansy for a day then. Udell was working right next door to Black and Tan.
The piano player, Udell?
Yeah, he was working next door to Black and Tan. Working for Beansy at E-Lights at two clarinets, William for myself. Yeah, two clarinets.
How did that work out when you had two clarinets? How would you play? Would you read? Could you fake together? No, we'd fake together.
Fake together. I'm gonna have Charlie Love on trumpet. When he was sober. Yeah, when he was sober, he might not come there at all. That's when we had two clarinets.
Well, would one play lower register and one play upper, or would you both play upper and hominets?
Both of us would play up. Both of us would play down. We would play first and second though.
Mm-hmm. We could do that well.
A lot of numbers I didn't know how to play the second one. I'd play the lead.
We would have played the second. We had a nice band over there at the lights.

They had the lyrics theater that time. It was right on the corner. We had a nice band over there at the lights. And they had all those ministries coming in venison stuff come over there after the show, between shows, and the show was out around 11, 30, 12 o'clock at night, unless we was giving a midnight ramble. We had a lot of musicians used to come in there from off, out of town musicians used to build the shows, come in, stop there, listen, a lot of them used to come in and sit in. Old man John Robichaud, he had a band at the Lyrics Theatre. You don't remember Red Happy, you don't know who he talked about?
I never knew him, but I heard a lot of guys talk about him.

Well, he was a summons on him, Red Happy. He used to, he was with John Robichaud. Oh man. He was a fine drummer, this guy, Black Benny, was a fine drummer. He got killed, a poison or something. I think he got killed. He had some nice trumpet players around here like Buddy Petit, Ricka, Rene, Chris Kelly, Lee Collins, Alvin Alcorn, Manny Mineta.
What are these different guys specialize in?

Oh, they all practice players just like, except Buddy Petit. He had his own style of playing. That's where Lewis got a lot of his artists from Buddy Petit. He got a lot of artists from Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly. This fellow, Dude Foster. He never played nothing hard. He never went out of the staff. Everything he played was right down on the staff. But he was a wonderful man. He was a wonderful man. When he stood in his sober. He drank too, huh? Oh yeah. And then he used to take three and four jobs for one night. He drank too, huh? Oh yeah. And then he used to take three and four jobs for one night. Everybody be looking for Buddy to come with stuff stuff with ain't nobody. He was one of the luckiest musicians ever lived though. Because I know people be looking for him with pistol to kill him and when they see him they don't do him nothing. He laugh and lie right on out of it. Now we had some fine trombone players around here. The guy was, I think was the best trombone player was a father called Yank. He lived across the river. He died. He used to play with Sam Morgan. He was another Louis Armstrong. He never missed. Never hit nothing unless he was gonna make it. And he never tried nothing unless he was gonna make it. Yank was a wonderful trombone man.

Say I wanted to show you this picture. That's what I've been looking for. Here's Earl Hines. Here's his sack section here. What is it? Uh... My glass. I was wondering if this was the guy. Any of these guys. That looks like Omar Simeon to me there. I don't know who that is. It's peach me.
It looks something like Paul Bones, eh? Mmhmm. I know it isn't though. No, that's not him though.
Well, I'll find a picture of the guy.
I'm trying to think of his name.
I think it's Don L. Howard, but I'm not sure.
No, I think his name is Simeon or Simeon. Simeon?
Something like that. Omar Simeon?
Something like that, I think.
Was he born and brought up there?
I believe he was from around here. Yeah, I think he's from around here. But he left from around here before I come here.
Here's Don L. Howard when he was playing with King Oliver. That's not the guy there, huh?
Mmhmm. No, no. I see Big Odd there too. Is that Big Odd set aside?
Yeah, that's Albert Nicholas and Bonnie McCullough.
Yeah, man. But you see that was Lewis' band before he left New Orleans. Albert Nicholas, Big Odd, uh, uh, uh.
Oh, yeah.
Uh, this guy named playing piano. What, uh. What's the guy from here?
Russell.
Oh, Lewis Russell.
Lewis Russell.
Yeah, Albert Louis' band. Before he left Youngwood with Oliver. Mmhmm. They were around there on Ramport Street. Played at Tom Anderson's. He left them with, uh, with, uh, Oliver.
Was Tom Anderson's a very, uh, jumping place? What happened there?

Well, that was about the most exclusive place they had around here at that time. Uh, Tom Anderson. Uh, Tom Anderson. Uh, it stayed back because, uh, we had another place there on, uh, Bienville between Ramport and Burgundy. Oh, I forgot, I forgot the name of the place. But anyway, that was where Manuel, uh, what's the name, Manuel Pures or somebody. Uh, I think, uh, who was playing trumpet around there. Uh, like, Big O was playing drums. And, uh, there's this girl, Sadie playing, uh, not Sadie. Uh, uh, Emma Barrett playing piano. Uh, who else was around there? Somebody else was around there playing. Uh, they kept a pretty nice crowd, but Tom Anderson was the leading place around here. At that time they only had, uh, Tom, uh, Tom Anderson in that block. The rest of that was all empty. There had a big Coca-Cola sign there on the corner of Ramport and Canal where that big, uh, five, ten cents to is. Nothing but a big Coca-Cola sign there at that time. All that was a big empty lot. Uh, the cars used to come up straight up, uh, Ramport Street to Canal Street and turn the trolley around and go back down to, uh, Industrial Canal or somewhere down there. And I was like, I went back down. Uh, on Sunday we used to have, uh, what they call an all-day picnic out at the lake. Used to have a train called Smokey Mary. I heard of it.
Yeah, man, you could run and keep up with that train though. Walk fast, you could keep up with it.

Honestly, you didn't carry it with four or five coaches on it. I wish you should have needed about seven or eight cause it was packed and jammed all the time. I would get out to the lake around 9, 30, 10 o'clock. And we'd walk about two blocks out on those piers to get to the pier, out on the wharf to get to the pier. And we'd get out there and we'd start playing about 10 o'clock and play until 5 o'clock that evening. And they had at least five bands out there every Sunday. A different wharf. Right here they got a band, right there they got another, another, another. Every time you turn around you could hear a trumpet blowing through the wind at each other.
Were they trying to buck each other?

Oh man, buck. Buck all day long. And after they get full of that whiskey and wine, man, they buck all day. I used to be, Tom Albert used to be out there. But he didn't never buck none of them cause he couldn't play with them fellas. Letting him play some music. Now he was at home when you put some music in front of him. But other than that, I used to take his plays when they go to Bopper. I go to the winder too. He'd be at the winder blowing the trumpet, I'd beat the winder with my clarinet. He's the hell. Who'd be out there?
Oh man, they'd have a gang of people.
Yeah. Oh man, they'd have a gang of people.

like if you had a little club and you either buy one of those camps out there, a lot of people bought them out there. As a matter of fact, a lot of people used to live out there all the summer. You could rent one of those places for the day. They had stoves out there, they had beds, you could get and lock up one of them with your friend, go to bed, you could dance and you could swim, dining room, eat. A lot of guys used to bring their food out there and cook it out there and then a lot of them used to cook it at home and bring it from baskets. They used to have a lot of fun out there. They had water swimming, they would swim until they get tired and come dance until they get tired and go back swimming. They have a lot of fun. They used to have a keg built. They have sometimes 14 kegs of building. Everybody get drunk, fall overboard. I don't see more people fall overboard. I'm heading up. Trying to walk that wall from the land into that thing, fall right in that water. Put you in. Somebody got to go there and get them out. Well, how deep was the water? Oh, about a few. Anybody get drowned in it.
Just up to your way, son. Well, it might so well.

Yeah, some of them. Some of them. Then some of them used to just jump in there for fun and get drunk like that. Just jump in the water. Close and watch everything. Load it, tennis. Jump overboard. I used to like to play out there. It used to get me to go to Moss Point, Mississippi. Play that Saturday night. We got to catch that first train out of there. Pass it through there around four something in the morning. Then you get in here around seven thirty something to eat. And we got to be out there at the lake at nine. To go scuffling in. No sleep. That's when you get to around two o'clock in the evening. Everybody's gone swimming and nobody in there. But got a couple old people sitting around there eating sandwiches or drinking or something like that. They don't want to dance. I mean, you get tired of just sitting there playing to the walls and that sleep coming down on you. But it's tough. Then you got to get up and walk around, go get some ice water, wash your face. Try to get yourself straight down. And the beatiness thing, then you have to go play it at the Caporato Hall at night. Oh man. Oh the economy hall. Oh man. And when you get there, the people in there like that. They want nothing but them old blues all night long. If they don't want the blues, you play something. You don't never play too fast for them. They ain't like it at night. You could play fast. You want that. That was one step for them. You used to play shotties, cakewalks, all those things. They have the prize for the best waltzer, and the prize for the best shotties dancer, prize for the best cakewalk dancer. Play all that play. Through the night of the dance. And then from there, on Monday night, they go to Pantitula. Another dance there. And then you might rest Tuesday night. Wednesday night, you go to Tibidó. Play a jitney dance there. So it's the night you go to Racelet. You play a jitney dance there. Friday night, we play at the Fryman's Hall in West Wego. Saturday night, we gone back to Moss Point Recipe or Gulfport, one of them places.
We used to play so much to attend the troops. Send somebody in our place sometimes.
Albert Morgan was playing baseball with us. Him and I were taking a vacation with Chicago. Just got tired of it. We stayed in Chicago a week. And come back. After we done got about broke. stuff
